title: Rules vs Learning - How Each System Works
summary: Two features - where the logic comes from and how a system handles something new - let you classify any everyday system as rule-based or learning.
objectives: Distinguish a rule-based system from a learning system using two clear features.
Give one everyday example of each and explain the difference.
Use the terms rule-based, learning, data and model accurately.

body: Two machines can do the same job in totally different ways. Today you learn the two features that reveal which is which - and you will never be fooled by a shiny screen again.

sections.label: The difference you are looking for
sections.heading: Two ways a system can reach an answer
sections.altText: Two columns. A rule-based system takes an input, follows a rule a person wrote, and gives an output. A learning system takes labelled examples, finds a pattern itself, and uses that pattern on a new input.
sections.caption: Both give an answer. The difference is **where the rule came from** — a person wrote it, or the system found it.

left.title: Rule-based system
steps: Follow the rule a person wrote

right.title: Learning system
steps: Use it on a new input

terms.definition: Logic written by a person as fixed steps.
A system that builds a model from data instead of fixed rules.
The labelled examples a learning system is shown.
The pattern a learning system builds from its data.
A true characteristic you use to classify a system, not a surface look.

sections.heading: Two features that decide it
body: **Feature one** - where does the logic come from? In a [[rule-based system]] a person writes it. In a [[learning system]] it comes from data.
**Feature two** - what happens with something new? A rule-based system only handles cases its rules cover. A learning system can handle new cases that look like its examples.

sections.heading: Data is not the model
body: Be careful with words. The [[data]] is the examples. The [[model]] is the pattern built from them. Change the data and you can change the model.
A learning system does not understand meaning - it matches patterns. Always check its answers.

sections.label: Let's try it - hands-on
body: Build the feature chart, then use it to classify everyday systems you meet in the UAE.
items: Add an example to each row.
Underline the feature that decided each answer.
Write two sentences using data and model correctly.

items: Which feature is the strongest proof of a learning system?

worksheet.title: Week 2 Core worksheet - Rules vs Learning - How Each System Works

questions.prompt: A metro ticket gate opens only when a valid card is tapped. An engineer wrote out every condition the gate checks before it opens. Which classification and reason is correct?

options.text: Rule-based, because a person wrote the logic the gate follows.
Learning, because it builds a model from the thousands of cards tapped each day.
Rule-based, because the gate is simple and does not have a modern screen.
Learning, because it deals with a new passenger it has never seen before.

feedback.correct: Exactly - the deciding feature is where the logic came from, and here a person wrote it as fixed steps.
feedback.incorrect: Handling lots of taps, or looking plain, are surface traits; what decides it is that a person wrote the conditions rather than the system finding them in data.

questions.prompt: Each clue below is evidence about a system. Match each clue to what it proves about that system.

left.text: You can open the file and read every step the machine follows, written out by its maker.
The system was shown thousands of labelled examples before it worked at all.
It refuses any case its maker did not write a step for.
It handled a phrase correctly that nobody had ever typed into it before.

right.text: Rule-based: the logic came from a person.
Learning: the logic came from data.
Rule-based: it only handles cases its rules cover.
Learning: it handles new cases that look like its examples.

feedback.correct: You used both features: where the logic came from, and what happens when something new arrives.
feedback.incorrect: Two clues are about where the logic came from and two are about what happens with a new case - sort them by which feature each one is really telling you about.

questions.prompt: Select every piece of evidence that would be good proof that a system is a learning system.

options.text: It was shown labelled examples before it could do the job.
It gets new cases right that look like its examples.
Changing the examples it was shown changes the answers it gives.
Its screen is colourful and it updates every month.
It gives its answer almost instantly.
A person wrote out every step it follows.

feedback.correct: All three are about data building the logic - that is real proof, unlike how the system looks or how fast it is.
feedback.incorrect: Speed and a modern look are surface traits, and a person writing every step is proof of the opposite; pick the clues that point to data building the logic.

questions.prompt: True or false: because a shopping app looks modern and changes its layout often, we can be sure it is a learning system.

feedback.correct: Right - looking modern is a surface trait, and a rule-based system can be given a shiny new layout at any time.
feedback.incorrect: A new look tells you nothing about where the logic came from; you would need evidence that the system built its logic from examples.

questions.prompt: A spellchecker flags a word only when that word is missing from a fixed list its makers typed in. Complete the classification sentence.
questions.stem: This is a {{1}} system, because a {{2}} wrote the logic.

feedback.correct: A fixed list typed in by its makers is logic written by a person, so this is rule-based.
feedback.incorrect: Ask where the logic came from: nobody showed this spellchecker labelled examples - a person typed the list, so it is rule-based.

formative.targets: Directly checks 'recognises the difference between rule-based and learning systems'
formative.check: Exit ticket: classify two systems and give the feature that distinguishes them
formative.successCriteria: Correctly classifies both and names a distinguishing feature (not a surface trait).
formative.evidence: Exit slips sorted secure / partial / not-yet.
